prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, which brought atomic time and frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock first, and the reading of the other seven openings has strengthened rather than weakened that view. It is the only shortlisted candidate that every one of the eight members ranked, and it is top-five for five of us, so the support is broad and not driven by a single subfield. On the substance, the magic-wavelength idea lets one interrogate a very large number of neutral atoms with Doppler and recoil effects suppressed, and that is what moved fractional uncertainty from the 1e-16 regime to 1e-18 and made statistical averaging fast enough to be useful. The evidence is experimental and independent: JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and others have reproduced and surpassed each other, and clock-to-clock comparisons including optical fibre links are routine. It also meets my test of whether a method opens new ways of observing nature: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, searches for variation of constants and for dark-matter couplings, relativistic geodesy, and a likely redefinition of the second. The credit chain is short and defensible: Katori for the lattice concept and first demonstrations, Ye for taking it to the accuracy and stability frontier and linking it to the comb.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution and overlap. Strontium lattice clocks were developed in parallel by several groups (Lemonde at SYRTE, Sterr and Schmidt at PTB, Takamoto and Katori at Tokyo, Ludlow and Bloom at NIST/JILA), and Ye's best results rest on frequency-comb and laser-stabilisation technology that the 2005 prize already honoured. Ion clocks (Wineland, 2012, and Rosenband's Al+ clock) are a competing line of precision timekeeping, so a committee could ask whether this is a distinct step or an incremental refinement of recognised work. There is also a timing argument: the redefinition of the second has not happened, and waiting for it would give a cleaner narrative. I do not find that last point compelling, since the performance is already confirmed by many groups.

responses.point: Eva Lindroth ranks the optical lattice clock first, as I do, stressing that it is simple to explain, rests on well-understood atomic structure and is reproduced in many laboratories, while noting that Katori and Ye are the two clear principals.
responses.response: I agree with the core and want to add a qualification from the experimental side. Simplicity of the idea should not hide how much the 1e-18 result owes to cryogenic or blackbody-radiation control, ultrastable cavities and the comb link, which is mostly Ye's contribution and not Katori's original concept. That supports a pair rather than Katori alone. Where I would push you is on the ion-clock overlap: the 2012 prize covered single-ion quantum control, and the Al+ clock was a demonstration of that line. I think we should say explicitly in the citation that the achievement is the many-atom neutral lattice scheme, so the committee is not seen as recognising timekeeping twice.

responses.point: Bernhard Mehlig puts topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect first and the clock second, valuing a simple, universal and well-understood idea, and sees the clock as conceptually clean with timely recognition.
responses.response: I understand the appeal of a universal organising principle, and the Z2 classification plus the HgTe edge-transport measurement is a strong chain. But I would qualify the claim that it is simply timelier. Topological phases were recognised in 2016, and the credited trio omits Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, whose HgTe proposal is what made Molenkamp's experiment possible; I would not know how to defend that omission outside the committee. The clock has a shorter and tighter credit chain. I also disagree with the implicit weighting of understanding over observation: a clock that improves by two orders of magnitude and opens new measurements of gravity and constants is a comparable kind of achievement. I would not object strongly if B007 ends up in a two-part prize, but the union of names would exceed three.

responses.point: Eva Olsson ranks spherical-aberration correction first, arguing that attribution is clean among Rose, Haider and Urban, that the instrument is commercially standard and independently reproduced, and that it was a long-standing omission.
responses.response: I agree that B032 has the cleanest credit chain on the shortlist and I ranked it third for the same reasons, as a method that opens new observation of nature. My reservations are two. First, Krivanek's independent STEM corrector work is a real omission that the credited trio cannot address, which is a difficulty if the committee wants a fair account of who removed the Scherzer limit. Second, I ask what is physics here and what is instrumentation for other fields; the clock also shifts what physics can be tested, while corrected microscopy mostly serves materials science and chemistry. That is not disqualifying, since I value instruments that open new observation, but I would want the citation to lead with the physical limit overcome. I am open to B032 as an alternative if the clock stalls.

responses.point: Mark Pearce ranks the IceCube neutrino discovery first as a new observational window and a decades-long instrument achievement, with Halzen and Karle as a defensible pair, and ranks the clock fifth as mature with repeated independent comparisons.
responses.response: IceCube is a genuine discovery of a new window, and I take that seriously. My concern is attribution and what the prize would really credit. A cubic-kilometre detector and its analyses are the work of a very large collaboration with an AMANDA lineage; two names would leave out the people who established ice optics and calibration, and the source-identification picture is still developing, as several of us noted. The clock has a more compact set of principals and a complete, independently confirmed record. I do not dismiss your point that the field is stable and mature, but I would ask whether the diffuse-flux discovery by itself is where the committee wants to place the citation, or whether it is better to wait for stronger source associations.

uncertainties: Whether the committee would treat Katori and Ye as sufficient or want to account for parallel strontium-clock work at SYRTE, PTB and NIST, which cannot fit within three names.
Whether the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize make the clock look like a continuation of already recognised precision-spectroscopy work.
Whether to prefer waiting for the formal redefinition of the second, which I judge unnecessary but others may weigh differently.
Relative standing of atom interferometry (B034) if Chu's earlier 1997 recognition is read as having already covered the main light-pulse achievement.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B056 (no link to Katori, Ye or their laboratories). I note for transparency that I am a Lund atomic physicist in the same broad AMO community, that I know the quantum-memory field (relevant to B023, which is not in my preferred configuration) closely, and that WACQT leadership overlaps institutionally with Göran Johansson's Chalmers, which bears on B058 rather than on the clock.
